title: Owning Mahowny
full_review:
A mild-mannered assistant bank manager embezzles millions from his job to maintain his out-of-control gambling habit in the cautionary "Owning Mahowny" (Sony Classics). Based on actual events which took place in 1982 -- documented in Gary Ross' best seller "Stung" -- director Richard Kwietniowski scores big with this well-crafted character study of one man's downward spiral of addiction.

By day, Dan Mahowny (Philip Seymour Hoffman) is an unassuming employee of a large Toronto bank -- a glorified paper pusher with a knack for numbers. By night, however, Mahowny is a high roller with a compulsion for ponies and college sports, which lands him in debt to a local bookie (Maury Chakin) to the tune of ten grand.

When his dedication at the office garners him a promotion, the bank's limitless coffers are effectively put at his disposal. Mahowny wastes no time in using his new position to siphon money from the bank in order to cover his bets. He scheme proves effective, but also facilitates his free-fall into further debt.

In a delusional effort to score big and wipe his slate clean, Mahowny hops a jet to Atlantic City with a suitcase full of company cash. Once there, his jinxed wagering quickly raises the antenna of Victor Foss (John Hurt), the casino's manager who becomes intrigued with Mahowny.

Deflated, he returns to Toronto where he is confronted by his doting girlfriend, Belinda (Minnie Driver), who, though remaining naively aloof about the scope of his problem and his ill-fated scheme, is growing alarmed by their strained relationship. He placates her with promises of a trip to Vegas -- where he wins big and loses bigger.

Mahowny's placidity is shattered by suspicious findings during a routine bank audit, as well as a mounting police investigation. With no way out from under his now-staggering debt, Mahowny travels back to Atlantic City. And while Lady Luck smiles on him, her fickleness proves the house always wins in the end.

Viewing Mahowny's self-destruction is like rubbernecking past a car wreck -- tragic, but too irresistible to turn away from. Kwietniowski pulls no punches in presenting him as a pathetic loser, but what makes Mahowny's demise utterly more fascinating than some garden-variety crack addict's is the ingenuity involved in his downfall. Even the vilest criminals deserve a few extra points for being clever. Mahowny is the ultimate underdog antihero, an unethical David who takes on the twin Goliaths of casinos and the banking industry and -- for a brief time -- wins. His morally bankrupt actions are remarkable, though by no means laudable.

Due to sporadic rough language and vulgarities as well as fleeting nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
